verification_vocabulary: As GRAPH-FORMAT.md: bibliographic_metadata_checked = identity/edition checked against the named record; supporting_page_checked = an abstract, description, contents page or opening pages were read for the point in the note; unverified = not cited. No book was read in full. Claims about a work's argument rest only on what the note says was read.
shared_ids_note: Source ids use the prefix cdng_ and are shared across the four drafts cdn_national_tradition, cdn_political_national, who_killed_debate and cdn_regional; one id means one record. ind127_harris_1997 is an existing atlas source.

records.citation: P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.

verification.checked_against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (citation line on p. 4)
verification.note: Pages 4–5 read: Cook coined "limited identities" (1967) and Careless popularized it (1969); before the 1960s historians emphasized "the economic and political unity of Canada as it evolved from a colony into an independent nation-state"; "liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill, and … conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey"; the approach was "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States"; Cook and Careless embraced limited identities partly in response to Quebec separatism; Atlantic historians espoused it for other reasons. The rest of the essay is unread. Paragraphs 4–6 read on 2026-10-12 after the Sol review: Ken Windsor "initiated and eloquently defended the creation of a journal"; David Earl showed it would be viable; Buckner "agreed to become the editor"; the title was revived from David Russell Jack's journal (1901–08).

records.claim: Characterizes the national tradition and the origin of limited identities.
